precepts.text: Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness. We spend a lot of time restoring brothers and sisters that fall, bringing them back up, making them better than they used to be. We do it for everybody else.
precepts.point: Is not this thy fear, thy confidence, thy hope, and the uprightness of thy ways? A lot of men walk around saying I am not scared, I will die for this truth. But the real fear goes into unresolved trauma, unresolved issues, things in our past we have not overcome. When we get faced with a challenge, we turn back into that little kid, that boy, that boyfriend that got cheated on, that past marriage.

note.label: This Woman's Work

precepts.why:
Eliphaz says to Job, “Behold, thou hast instructed many, and thou hast strengthened the weak hands.” A lot of brothers go out and teach, some at camp 30 days in a row, 100 days, 365 days. We strengthen the weak hands: people come into the body sick and needing help, marriages come in messed up, and we dedicate our time to figuring out how to fix them.

That is Galatians 6:1: “Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.” Brothers will fall, sisters will fall, people in the congregation will fall, and we spend a lot of our time restoring them, bringing them back up, getting them back in position and making them better than they used to be. We do it for everybody else.

As a leader in this truth your phone rings all day: can I counsel with you, I've got a question. We answer, we deal with it, and when we don't know the answer we go to leadership and get counsel for their counsel. “Thy words have upholden him that was falling”: put the cigarettes down, bro; stop smoking weed; see, the Bible says this.

But the verse says, “considering thyself”. Inside our own household we don't do it. Our wife asks a question and we say, go watch 15 minutes with the captains. We deal with everything on the outside, but we are not teaching and building up our own possession. So when it comes upon us, “thou faintest; it toucheth thee, and thou art troubled.” You freeze up, you fold up, and you go against your own counsel, because most men don't counsel about what is going on in their own household. The one who restores everybody else has to consider himself too.

precepts.text: Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap. If you decide to undermine the brother next to you or do deceitful stuff to your sister, it is going to come back to you. It might not be this year; it might be next year, but it is going to come.
precepts.point: Not only the Jews, but many also of other nations, took great indignation, and were much grieved for the unjust murder of the man, because Onias had a good report even among the other nations. The king was heartily sorry, and moved to pity, and wept, because of the sober and modest behaviour of him that was dead; and being kindled with anger, he took away Andronicus his purple, rent off his clothes, led him through the whole city unto that very place where he had committed impiety against Onias, and there slew he the cursed murderer. Thus the Lord rewarded him his punishment, as he had deserved.

note.label: From Brother To Betrayer

precepts.why:
“Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.” Don't be deceived, brothers and sisters. God is not mocked. Whatsoever you do in this earth, you are going to reap from what you have done.

So if you decide, I'm going to undermine my brother next to me, I'm going to do some deceitful stuff to my sister, it is going to come back to you. It might not be this year; it might be next year, but it is going to come.

That is the history of 2 Maccabees 4. Jason sowed undermining against his own brother and reaped being undermined by another, “compelled to flee into the country of the Ammonites.” Menelaus got the principality by flattery and money and went on to steal vessels of gold out of the temple, and Andronicus sowed deceit and murder against Onias and reaped death in that very place. Brothers turning on brothers for position all reap what they sow.

precepts.text: This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth; but thou shalt meditate therein day and night, that thou mayest observe to do according to all that is written therein: for then thou shalt make thy way prosperous. When we meditate on the scriptures day and night and do them, the Lord makes our way prosperous and gives the increase we desire, spiritually and emotionally, when we put our mind on the Lord.
precepts.point: Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap. When you put in the sin, the consequences are going to happen. For he that soweth to his flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption: you will be judged by it. But he that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting: when you sow yourself into the scriptures, the Lord gives blessings, favor, mercy, and abundance.

note.label: Satan's Kiss To Your Demise

precepts.why:
“he that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting.” When you sow yourself into the scriptures, the Lord is going to give you blessings: he will show you favor, have mercy on you, and give you abundance. That is Joshua 1:8: “This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth; but thou shalt meditate therein day and night.”

We should meditate on the scriptures day and night, “that thou mayest observe to do according to all that is written therein: for then thou shalt make thy way prosperous, and then thou shalt have good success.” Meditating and doing is the sowing.

When we do that, the Lord makes our way prosperous. He gives us the abundance we desire, spiritually, emotionally, all the increases we desire, when we put our mind on the Lord. That is reaping of the Spirit.

precepts.why:
“whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.” What you put in, you are going to reap. When you put in the sin, the consequences are going to happen, period. Paul says it plainly: “For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

Sin is death. That is the corruption reaped by the one who sows to his flesh: sow that sin to your flesh and you will be judged by it. And the gift of God, eternal life through Christ, is the “life everlasting” reaped by the one who sows to the Spirit.

What you put in, you are going to receive as a reward. Wages for sin, a gift for the one who sows to the Spirit. God is not mocked.

precepts.why:
The Lord set both harvests before Israel from the beginning: “I call heaven and earth to record this day against you, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life, that both thou and thy seed may live.”

What you put in, you are going to get; you are going to receive a reward. Life and blessing for the one who sows to the Spirit, death and cursing for the one who sows to his flesh. Heaven and earth are called as witnesses, so no one can say he was not told. God is not mocked.

And the choice reaches past you: choose life “that both thou and thy seed may live.” What a man sows, his children reap with him.

But as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.

“whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.” Choose the Lord, sow to the Spirit, and of the Spirit reap life everlasting.

precepts.text: If a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual restore such an one in the spirit of meekness. You got to build and restore this man back to life, speak life into that brother to get him back on track. Bear ye one another's burdens; if we was in that same situation, we would want our brothers to come and get us out of it.
precepts.point: His three friends came every one from his own place to mourn with him and to comfort him, and sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him, for they saw that his grief was very great. Now you see the type of men that you're around; that is true friendship.

note.label: Character & Integrity: The Hidden Strength Behind Wisdom

precepts.why:
Job's three friends heard of all the evil that came upon him, came every one from his own place “to mourn with him and to comfort him”, and “sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great.” Now you see the type of men you are around. That is true friendship, and Galatians shows what it is supposed to do.

“Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.” When a brother falls, you have to build and restore this man back to life. Speak life into that brother to get him back on track, in meekness, remembering you could be tempted too.

“Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.” If we were in that same situation, we would want our brothers to come and get us out of it.

Job held fast his integrity when he lost his kids, lost everything he had, and had boils all over his body. Satan came in through his wife, “curse God, and die”, but Job answered, “shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?” A man going through that needs brothers who will sit with him, carry his burden with him and restore him, not tear him down.

precepts.text: Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.
precepts.point: Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others. Looking means acting when a brother struggles.

note.label: The Highway of the Upright: an Israelites's Strait Journey

precepts.why:
“Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves.” If I esteem you better than myself, then within my power I have to help you come up with a solution, or help provide it. “Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others.” That does not mean just looking: yeah, he's struggling like hell. No. Look means action. “Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus.” And Christ was no weak, effeminate man; he was a strong, powerful, upright man.

Paul says it plainly: “Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.” That is how we are going to rise. If twelve of you have cars that run fine and a brother in the body can't even fix his car, and you shut your mouth and do nothing, you are weak. That is not how our black men are supposed to stand. Israelites are commanded to help each other.

So every school should have its mechanics, carpenters, plumbers and electricians helping the people in the body, making videos so the next brother can do it too. Instead of paying $1,900 you pay $300 for the parts, and brothers with the spirit fix the car. That's alms deeds; that's helping your nation.

We used to have that. Black people used to speak to each other in the street because we had a commonality, a common struggle. Now we have fallen apart. Bearing one another's burdens is how the nation is gathered together and becomes an economic force: that is the mind of Christ and the law of Christ.

precepts.text: And it does not matter if they are a repentant Israelite or if they are in the world. You still have got to respect and honour them either way. Because remember, we have got to let our light shine. We have got to be the light to the Gentiles, the unrepentant of our people. Because at one point you were unrepentant too. As we have therefore opportunity — so as much as this opportunity arises — let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith. So we have got to do good to all men, those in the truth and those out of the truth. That goes back to Romans when it says live peaceably with all men.
precepts.point: You make an atonement for your sins when you do that. When you honour your father, that wipes away your sins. Let us see why.

note.label: Honor Thy Father & Thy Mother

precepts.why:
Honouring your father and mother does not depend on whether they are a repentant Israelite or still in the world. You still have to respect and honour them either way.

We have to let our light shine and be the light to the Gentiles, the unrepentant of our people, because at one point you were unrepentant too. Paul says, “As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith.” As much as the opportunity arises, we do good to all men, those in the truth and those out of the truth, and that includes the parents who raised us.

That goes back to Romans, where it says live peaceably with all men. So when Sirach says “Whoso honoureth his father maketh an atonement for his sins”, it is not only the father who is in the faith; doing good to your parents wherever they stand is the honour that brings that atonement.

precepts.text: If a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; that is how you win souls.
precepts.point: There is a way to correct: brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness. A soft answer turneth away wrath; you do not render evil for evil and blast a brother, you build him up with a humble mind, and that is how souls are won. The man gathering sticks got the reproof that fit that willful case; meekness fits the brother overtaken in a fault.

A soft answer turneth away wrath. You do not render evil for evil and blast a brother; you build him up with a humble mind, and that is how souls are won. The man gathering sticks got the reproof that fit that willful case; meekness fits the brother overtaken in a fault.

precepts.text: Taking up your cross does not mean buying a cross from the pawn shop to wear around your neck; every man shall bear his own burden, enduring his own tests in this truth with prayer and fasting.
precepts.point: How do we willingly offer ourselves to the Lord in the twenty-first century? By giving up whatever presents itself as an obstacle between us and the Lord. It may be father, mother, husband, wife, or children; it may be drugs, money, or working on the sabbath. If you willingly offer yourself, you will not let any stumbling block keep you from the Lord.

note.label: Judges 5: The Song of Deborah and Barak: A Willing People

precepts.why:
Taking up your cross does not mean buying a cross from the pawn shop to wear around your neck. “For every man shall bear his own burden.”

Your cross is your own burden: enduring your own tests in this truth with prayer and fasting. That is how a man willingly offers himself to the Lord today, as the people did in the days of Deborah and Barak.

points: Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted. You want to meet him with the fruits of the Spirit, to restore his spirit back and build him back.

All of us come in sick. Sometimes leaders, or brothers, and not just brothers, sisters in some cases, have expectations of people that you yourself are not able to meet, or have not done. You expect people to be you. And it does not mean that you allow people to run over you, or just commit sin and let it go. But it tells us in chapter 5 verse 22, the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, which is what I want, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance, against such there is no law. Sometimes you have to be patient with brothers. Brothers are in positions and they are rough with the people. They deal with them harshly and they themselves are not right. In some cases they are stealing, and they show no consideration or mercy towards another brother.

points: Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ. As a leader you have to care for the people. Bear people's burdens. Be considerate of their plights, what they are going through. Know how to talk. Some people you have to cut up. Some brothers are evil, I get it, and the scriptures tell us some you save with fear, some you save with compassion. In Jude, we know that. But I am talking about brothers that are harsh, roughness in their speech towards another brother. We have to understand we came in sick. Imagine all the hang-ups that you have that we do not know about, or that you do not know about me. And if God decided to deal with us, none of us would make it. You have to care about the plight of your people, the situation they are going through. Some brothers sin and they are really remorseful about the sins they committed. You try to restore them in a spirit of meekness.

points: Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault: a man commits a sin. Ye which are spiritual: you who are a righteous judge, a just judge. Restore such an one in the spirit of meekness.

Notice it did not say, when judgment comes, how long. Every case is not the same. You cannot treat every case the same, because every man does not have the same spirit. Some men, you might put them out for six months and they're okay; some men, that six months can destroy them. Be very careful with that. You cannot destroy them.

Considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted. Let's say you kicked that man out for a year, and a couple of years later you commit that same sin. Would you want to be cut off for a year? When you pass judgment as a judge, consider yourself. It's not about get out, get out. None of us in this commission is perfect. The righteous man falls seven times and gets back up again. We will make mistakes. When that brother shows up in front of you as a judge, consider the judgment before you pass it: if it was you, would you want that same judgment?

Now, officers: a man is overtaken in a fault, judgment is passed, the brother is put out. What is the protocol? It is not simply no communication. The protocol is to assign an officer over that man. The man that's put out must contact that officer, not the other way around: updating him, watching classes, sending his notes. Then that officer follows up with leadership on what's going on with that man. If you put him out and say no contact whatsoever, how would you be able to restore him? You're not checking him to make sure he can be restored. The body is no contact, but you set an officer over him. That's why at the bottom it says restore such an one: he keeps contact with the man you appointed, and the man gives you a report: he's studying, he's doing this. That's how you restore him.

And it is the man who messed up who does the calling. I heard a man say, I'm the one supposed to be called. No: who messed up, me or you? You have to fix it. And how do you fix it? By contacting that officer; that officer gives you scriptures; you talk; what are you doing to fix the situation? That's the breakdown of that scripture.
